definitions.explanation: In Buddhism, mental states such as greed, anger, and delusion that cause suffering and hinder enlightenment. In everyday usage, refers more broadly to temptations and desires that are hard to resist.

examples.japanese: ダイエット{中|ちゅう}なのに{甘|あま}い{物|もの}が{食|た}べたい。{煩悩|ぼんのう}だらけだ。
examples.english: I want to eat sweets even though I'm on a diet. I'm full of temptations.

examples.japanese: {大晦日|おおみそか}の{除夜|じょや}の{鐘|かね}は{百八|ひゃくはち}つの{煩悩|ぼんのう}を{払|はら}うために{百八回|ひゃくはっかい}{鳴|な}らされる。
examples.english: The New Year's Eve bell is rung 108 times to dispel the 108 worldly desires.

notes:
{煩悩|ぼんのう} originates from Buddhist terminology. In Buddhist thought, there are traditionally 108 {煩悩|ぼんのう}, which is why the {除夜|じょや}の{鐘|かね} (New Year's Eve bell) is rung 108 times.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {煩悩|ぼんのう}を{捨|す}てる (to abandon worldly desires)
- {煩悩|ぼんのう}を{断|た}つ (to cut off worldly desires)
- {煩悩|ぼんのう}に{打|う}ち{勝|か}つ (to overcome temptation)
- {煩悩|ぼんのう}だらけ (full of worldly desires)

USAGE NOTES:
While the word comes from serious Buddhist philosophy, it is commonly used in a light, self-deprecating way in everyday speech — for example, when someone cannot resist food or shopping. The humorous tone acknowledges human weakness without deep religious connotation.
